Cell Signaling & Molecular Pharmacology Lab · Yonsei University

How do cells read chemicals?

Cells are constantly exposed to metabolites, drugs, hormones, and sensory molecules. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) help cells decide what those chemicals mean. We ask three simple questions: What does a receptor sense? Which pathway does it choose? And can we redesign that choice to control cell function?

We answer these questions with GPCRome-scale screening and quantitative signaling assays, then use receptor engineering, structural insight, and computation to turn mechanisms into new ligands and chemogenetic tools.

Research questions

Sense · Choose · Control

A chemical arrives. A receptor senses it. The receptor chooses a pathway. The cell changes its behavior. We study the rules behind each step — and use those rules to discover new ligands and build new ways to control signaling. Across these questions, we are particularly interested in GPCRs that connect chemical sensing to physiology, including receptors that shape itch, pain, and related sensory responses.

01

Sense — Which chemicals does a receptor recognize?

Chemical sensing · ligand selectivity · target identification · GPCR screening

We discover which chemicals activate or block GPCRs, and why some receptors recognize one molecule but not another. Target-focused and GPCRome-scale screens give us the first hit; concentration–response testing, orthogonal assays, and receptor counter-screens tell us whether that interaction is real and selective. We are especially interested in understudied, sensory, and orphan GPCRs whose chemical biology is still poorly understood.

GPCRome screeningligand discoverytarget deconvolutionreceptor selectivity
02

Choose — Which signaling pathway does a receptor activate?

G protein selectivity · non-canonical coupling · β-arrestin · signaling bias

Binding a ligand is only the beginning. Once a GPCR turns on, it can choose among several intracellular partners and produce very different outcomes. We map those choices with a 14-Gα BRET panel together with β-arrestin, cAMP, and Ca2+ assays. This lets us uncover non-canonical coupling, signaling bias, partial or inverse agonism, and allosteric effects — and ask why the same receptor behaves differently with different ligands or in different molecular contexts.

14-Gα profilingTRUPATH / BRETβ-arrestincAMP / Ca²⁺
03

Control — Can we redesign receptors to control cell function?

Chemogenetics · DREADDs · receptor engineering · precise control of signaling

Once we understand what a receptor senses and which pathway it chooses, we can begin to change those rules. We combine receptor mutagenesis, ligand profiling, structural insight, and iterative screening to build receptor–ligand systems with new selectivity or signaling behavior. Chemogenetic receptors turn this idea into a practical tool: a defined drug can control a defined receptor and, in turn, a defined cellular function.

chemogeneticsreceptor engineeringsynthetic pharmacologymechanism-guided design

Principal investigator

Hye Jin Kang, Ph.D.

Hye Jin Kang is an Associate Professor in the Department of Biotechnology at Yonsei University. Her research asks how GPCRs recognize chemical signals, choose intracellular pathways, and can be engineered to control cell function.

Her lab combines receptor-scale screening, quantitative pharmacology, molecular engineering, and structural and computational approaches.
